blindSummary:
This is a serious-risk destination for transgender visitors. Two provisions of the 1883 penal code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and an international legal-aid organisation lists this country among those criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and impersonation provisions against trans people. An international commission of jurists has described the national police as the leading perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals — harassment, arbitrary detention and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 administrative circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. The capital has a small organised community and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under impersonation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.
blindOutOfScope: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; the legal-gender-recognition circular's limits are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): two penal-code provisions criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women); prosecutions limited but harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services are frequent; no comprehensive anti-discrimination protections; authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence - widely condemned as torture. Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).
NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying international legal-aid trust's country profile documents this country's criminalisation of same-sex activity.

Opinion piece (Aug 2023) by a legal scholar at an international jurists' body: trans rights here currently rest on an administrative circular rather than law - the national police are described as the leading perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals, and in recent months both the police and the national human-rights commission acknowledged this; argues circulars are insufficient without legal reform.

A foreign home ministry's country-of-origin information note for asylum determinations on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (v6.0, Sept 2024): assessment of risk from state and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.
A foreign government's annual human-rights country report: official assessment including the SOGI section - criminalisation under the penal code and police harassment of LGBT persons.

Joint civil-society stakeholder report to the UN periodic review (3rd cycle) by a coalition of national advocacy organisations: documents criminalisation and human-rights violations against LGBTIQ individuals in this country.

A foreign immigration tribunal's response to an information request (Jan 2012): treatment of sexual minorities in this country - the principal penal-code provision criminalises 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' (up to 10 years, men only); a separate 'gross indecency' provision covers both sexes (amended in 1995 to cover women); rarely enforced with no convictions, but the tribunal notes criminalisation paves the way for police and anti-gay groups to treat all lesbian, bisexual and transgender people as criminals.
blindLocalsOnly: The 2016 recognition circular (not law) is a resident-facing instrument.
blindTangential: The penal-code provisions criminalising same-sex activity (up to 10 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the vagrancy and impersonation provisions are the trans-specific enforcement vehicle.
